sections.title: How does the Amdahl's law calculator work?
sections.html:
The Amdahl's law calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports task proportion (p) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the speedup factor (s), the speedup (S), the original time and the optimization factor (O).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Amdahl's law calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Task proportion (p)=speedup factor (s) × (optimization factor (O) − speedup (S)) ÷ (speedup (S) × (optimization factor (O) − speedup factor (s)))
Improved time=original time ÷ speedup (S)
Task proportion (p)=(maximum speedup (Smax) − 1) ÷ maximum speedup (Smax)
Improved time=original time × (1 − time percentage change)
Task proportion #1=speedup factor #1 × (theoretical speedup (S) of your parallel tasks − 1) ÷ (theoretical speedup (S) of your parallel tasks × (speedup factor #1 − 1))
Speedup factor #2=task proportion #2 × speedup factor #1 × theoretical speedup (S) of your parallel tasks ÷ (task proportion #1 × speedup factor #1 × theoretical speedup (S) of your parallel tasks − task proportion #1 × theoretical speedup (S) of your parallel tasks + task proportion #2 × speedup factor #1 × theoretical speedup (S) of your parallel tasks − speedup factor #1 × theoretical speedup (S) of your parallel tasks + speedup factor #1)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Amdahl's law calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the speedup factor, the speedup factor #1 and the speedup factor #3 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Amdahl's law calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns task proportion (p), derived from the speedup factor, the speedup factor #1 and the speedup factor #3. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Amdahl's law calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the speedup factor, the speedup factor #1, the speedup factor #3 and the speedup, which is 15 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter task proportion (p) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Task proportion (p) opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Amdahl's law calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
